paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a from-scratch generator and benchmark framework for verifiable numerical question answering (QA) over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO first synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + dense table contents) via an LLM, uses executable SQL queries on that source to produce gold answers, renders multiple perturbed non-relational views (pivots, hierarchical headers, merged cells, OCR-like noise, unit conversions, blanks, footnotes, etc.), and verbalizes the SQL into natural-language questions. It explicitly supports two evidence-flow topologies: parallel (extract one scalar per view, then aggregate) and sequential (lookup chains where intermediate results parameterize later views). The generator exposes controls over table count, attribute cardinalities, units, and perturbations, and records provenance masks so answers remain verifiable despite surface perturbations. The paper evaluates several LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen variants) on environmental and financial domains, shows steep accuracy degradations as table count and unit heterogeneity increase (especially for numerical/mixed-unit queries and multi-table inputs), demonstrates that GRADINO data can improve fine-tuning for scarce in-domain multi-table QA (complements small real datasets), and provides prompts, constraints, and generation details in the appendix.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Clear niche and motivation: the paper identifies a real blind spot—non-relational multi-table numerical reasoning—and motivates why existing relational benchmarks and post-hoc conversions are insufficient. 2) Methodological novelty and rigor: GRADINO decouples logical supervision (SQL on a latent relational source) from surface presentation, enabling verifiable answers while producing realistic non-relational perturbations. 3) Controlled, configurable generation: supports parallel vs sequential evidence flows, many perturbations, unit heterogeneity, and user-steerable semantic constraints. 4) Thorough empirical study: experiments across domains, table counts (up to 20), unit settings, and multiple LLMs; ablations show the compounding effect of table count + non-relationality + unit heterogeneity. 5) Practical utility: generated data helps fine-tune models and complements scarce real training data (e.g., combining GRADINO with GRI-QA improves performance). 6) Reproducibility and documentation: detailed prompts, constraint machinery, and generation statistics are provided in the appendix, and code/datasets are promised/released, which benefits the research community.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism gap: GRADINO is a controlled diagnostic generator by design and the authors acknowledge it may not capture all distributional, visual, or semantic regularities of real spreadsheets/reports (e.g., alignment cues, chart-table mixtures). This limits direct conclusions about deployed systems unless complemented with real-data evaluation. 2) Generation / evaluation LLM overlap: the internal generator uses gpt-5-mini while gpt-5-mini is also evaluated; although the paper discusses this and shows degradation across model families, using the same LLM for generation and testing raises potential bias concerns and should be explored further. 3) Narrow task scope: the focus is on numerical scalar extraction and aggregation; other common multi-table tasks (set operations, textual joins, open-ended aggregation, tree-shaped joins, and categorical reasoning) are not explored. 4) Simplifying assumptions in sequential chains: sequential QA enforces unique matches for intermediate lookups (one occurrence per lookup), which limits evaluation of more ambiguous or many-to-many join behaviors found in practice. 5) Question fidelity: NL questions are LLM-generated and—while mostly reliable—introduce some errors (notably more in sequential instances), relying on an LLM verifier/repair rather than fully guaranteed NL fidelity. 6) Limited model breadth: experiments use one closed strong model and several Qwen variants; broader model families (other open families, instruction tuned / chain-of-thought variants) could strengthen external validity.
comments_suggestions_typos: Suggestions to improve the paper: (a) Expand the real-table validation by adding more diverse real reports and, where feasible, human-annotated conversions so readers can better judge transfer to natural sources. (b) Add ablations that vary the generating LLM (e.g., use an open LLM to create latent sources/questions) to quantify any dependence on the generator. (c) Provide more detail / examples about the SMT constraint sampling edge cases (e.g., modulo or discrete domains) and how many candidates are discarded in practice per domain. (d) Consider a controlled experiment relaxing the unique-match assumption in sequential chains to probe ambiguity handling. (e) In the appendix/prompt descriptions, a few places repeat wording (minor copy edits) — a light proofread will tighten presentation. Overall the manuscript is well written and the appendix is thorough.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors provide an explicit limitations section and discuss ethical considerations: GRADINO uses synthetic, fictional entities (no PII), and the real-table validation uses public datasets. They acknowledge the benchmark is diagnostic rather than a full replacement for real curated data and warn against overinterpreting scores on synthetic instances. That said, I would have liked more discussion of deployment risks: (i) how a model optimized on GRADINO data might behave on messy real corporate reports (silent numerical errors in financial settings have real consequences), (ii) domain or language representation gaps if the generator is grounded primarily in English domain lexicons, and (iii) clearer guidelines for safe use in decision-making pipelines (e.g., recommended human-in-the-loop checks for numeric-sensitive outputs). Overall the paper's treatment of limitations and impact is good but could expand on operational deployment risks and multilingual concerns.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical violations detected. The authors avoid PII and use public tables for validation; they discuss data provenance and licenses. One note: the paper contains a meta-note about an LLM 'reviewing' and rewriting sections (and preferring its own paraphrases). This is interesting but raises questions about evaluative objectivity when models introspect on human text; the authors acknowledge this and it does not affect the technical contribution. Also, using a closed LLM for generation/evaluation may limit reproducibility for some researchers without API access—this is a practical, not ethical, concern.
